def: Connected with the sense of touch, or perceptible by touch.
ex: Mechanical keyboards offer enjoyable tactile feedback that many software engineers and writers prefer.
nat: Young children learn spatial concepts rapidly through hands-on tactile play activities.

mis.bad: The phone has an feedback tactile.
mis.good: The phone has tactile feedback.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "tactile feedback".

def: To contaminate or pollute something, or spoil someone's reputation or integrity.
ex: The bribery investigation threatened to taint the firm entire international business reputation.
nat: Avoid touching clean medical instruments with bare hands to avoid tainting them.

mis.bad: The news tainted with his good image.
mis.good: The news tainted his good reputation.
mis.why: "Taint" is transitive and takes a direct object without "with".

def: A completely different line of thought or action from the main topic.
ex: The speaker went off on a long tangent about his college days.
nat: Try to keep meetings focused and avoid going off on unrelated tangents.

mis.bad: He went to a tangent during his presentation.
mis.good: He went off on a tangent during his presentation.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "go off on a tangent".

def: To twist together into a confused or messy mass.
ex: Wired headphone cables always seem to tangle tightly inside my backpack pocket.
nat: New regulations created a bureaucratic tangle that delayed foreign business approvals.

mis.bad: My earphones tangled down inside my bag.
mis.good: My earphones tangled up inside my bag.
mis.why: Use the particle "up" with tangle: "tangled up".

def: To diminish or reduce gradually in thickness, width, or rate of occurrence.
ex: The economic stimulus program will gradually taper off over the next six months.
nat: The hiking trail began to taper into a narrow rocky footpath near the summit.

mis.bad: The rain is tapering down to stop.
mis.good: The rain is tapering off.
mis.why: The common phrasal verb meaning to decrease gradually is "taper off".

def: To lose luster, or harm someone's reputation or historical legacy.
ex: The scandal threatened to permanently tarnish the legacy of the respected university president.
nat: Silver jewelry will gradually tarnish when exposed to humid air and moisture.

mis.bad: This mistake tarnished in his career.
mis.good: This mistake tarnished his career.
mis.why: "Tarnish" takes a direct object without the preposition "in".

def: Sharp or acid in taste, or sharp and cutting in tone or remark.
ex: Fresh green apples give this homemade fruit pie a pleasantly crisp, tart flavor.
nat: She gave a tart reply when asked why the code review was late.

mis.bad: This fruit is very sour tart.
mis.good: This fruit has a pleasantly tart taste.
mis.why: Do not combine "sour" and "tart" redundantly; use "tart" for pleasant acidity.

def: To provoke or challenge someone with insulting or teasing remarks.
ex: Rival football fans continued to taunt the visiting goalkeeper after he conceded.
nat: Older siblings should never cruelly taunt younger children about their fears.

mis.bad: They taunted to the other team.
mis.good: They taunted the other team.
mis.why: "Taunt" takes a direct object without "to".

def: Too long, slow, or dull; tiresome or monotonous.
ex: Entering thousands of invoice records manually into the old spreadsheet was incredibly tedious.
nat: Writing unit tests can feel tedious, but it saves hours of debugging later.

mis.bad: I felt very tedious during the class.
mis.good: I felt very bored during the class / The class was tedious.
mis.why: Use "bored" for human feelings and "tedious" for the thing that causes boredom.

def: To be full of or swarming with living creatures or activity.
ex: The tropical coral reef teems with colorful marine species and vibrant sea anemones.
nat: Downtown streets teem with tourists and street performers on warm summer Friday evenings.

mis.bad: The forest teems of strange insects.
mis.good: The forest teems with strange insects.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "with" after "teem", not "of".

def: A person's or animal's nature, especially as it permanently affects their behavior.
ex: Working in emergency incident response requires a calm temperament under intense time pressure.
nat: The rescue dog has a wonderfully gentle temperament around young children and visitors.

mis.bad: He has an aggressive temperamental.
mis.good: He has an aggressive temperament.
mis.why: Use the noun "temperament" rather than the adjective "temperamental" here.

def: A violent windy storm, or violent commotion and emotional disturbance.
ex: The sailors fought bravely to keep their wooden vessel afloat during the fierce tempest.
nat: His sudden resignation created a fierce political tempest inside the party executive committee.

mis.bad: It was just a tempest in a cup of tea.
mis.good: It was just a tempest in a teapot.
mis.why: In American English, the idiom is "a tempest in a teapot" (storm in a teacup in UK).

def: A desire to do something, especially something wrong or unwise.
ex: I resisted the temptation to check work emails while enjoying my annual vacation.
nat: Fresh chocolate chip cookies on the counter presented an irresistible sweet temptation.

mis.bad: I fell in the temptation to buy it.
mis.good: I fell into temptation / succumbed to the temptation to buy it.
mis.why: Use "fall into temptation" or "succumb to temptation".

def: Tending to keep a firm hold of something; clinging or adhering closely.
ex: Her tenacious determination enabled her to overcome numerous career setbacks and launch her firm.
nat: The investigative journalist was tenacious in uncovering hidden offshore corporate financial accounts.

mis.bad: He is very tenaciously to solve bugs.
mis.good: He is very tenacious in solving bugs.
mis.why: Use the adjective "tenacious" followed by "in + -ing".

def: Gentleness and kindness, or the state of being tender to the touch.
ex: He spoke with unexpected tenderness when recalling memories of his beloved grandmother.
nat: The physician checked the patient abdominal area for any localized swelling or tenderness.

mis.bad: She showed a big tenderness to the baby.
mis.good: She showed great tenderness toward the baby.
mis.why: Use "great tenderness toward", not "a big tenderness to".

def: A principle or belief, especially one of the main principles of a philosophy.
ex: Respect for user privacy is a foundational tenet of our software engineering culture.
nat: Nonviolence was the central moral tenet guiding Gandhi civil rights movement.

mis.bad: This is one of the tenets principals.
mis.good: This is one of the principal tenets.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "principal tenets".

def: Stretched tight, or showing or causing nervous feelings of strain or worry.
ex: The atmosphere in the meeting room grew increasingly tense as quarterly losses were discussed.
nat: Doing deep breathing exercises helps relax tense shoulder and neck muscles after work.

mis.bad: I feel very tension about the presentation.
mis.good: I feel very tense about the presentation.
mis.why: Use the adjective "tense" after feel, not the noun "tension".

def: Mental or emotional strain, or the state of being stretched tight.
ex: Diplomatic tension between the neighboring countries eased following successful bilateral peace talks.
nat: Gentle stretching exercises can relieve physical tension built up in your lower back.

mis.bad: There is many tension in the office.
mis.good: There is a lot of tension in the office.
mis.why: "Tension" is uncountable here; use "a lot of tension" or "much tension", not "many".

def: Something that serves as tangible proof or clear evidence of a fact.
ex: The bridge survival during the massive earthquake is a testament to superior civil engineering.
nat: Her rapid career advancement is a true testament to her relentless work ethic.

mis.bad: This success is a testament of her effort.
mis.good: This success is a testament to her effort.
mis.why: The standard collocation is "testament to", not "testament of".

def: Relating to acting or the theater, or exaggerated and staged for effect.
ex: The defense attorney delivered an overly theatrical speech to influence the sequestered jury.
nat: Students rehearsed their major theatrical production for three months before opening night.

mis.bad: The movie had its launch theatrical yesterday.
mis.good: The movie had its theatrical release yesterday.
mis.why: Use the fixed phrase "theatrical release" for films shown in theaters.

def: Relating to heat; designed to retain heat or withstand high temperatures.
ex: Pack warm thermal underwear if you plan to go skiing in the Canadian Rockies.
nat: Modern data centers utilize sophisticated thermal imaging cameras to detect overheating server racks.

mis.bad: I bought a shirt thermal for winter.
mis.good: I bought thermal underwear / a thermal shirt for winter.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a thermal shirt".

def: A dense group of bushes or trees growing closely together.
ex: A frightened wild rabbit quickly darted into the thorny blackberry thicket for shelter.
nat: Hikers had to push through a dense thicket of bamboo along the trail.

mis.bad: He hid in a thick of trees.
mis.good: He hid in a thicket of bushes / trees.
mis.why: Use the specific noun "thicket" for a dense patch of small trees or shrubs.

def: A large, densely packed crowd of people or animals.
ex: An enthusiastic throng of spectators gathered outside the concert hall hours before doors opened.
nat: We had to push our way through a dense throng of holiday shoppers.

mis.bad: There was an immense throng in the street.
mis.good: There was a huge crowd / immense throng in the street.
mis.why: Pronounce "throng" with the voiceless "th" /θ/, not /t/.

def: To choke or strangle, or control and limit the rate of data flow.
ex: Our cloud infrastructure will automatically throttle incoming requests if traffic exceeds normal capacity limits.
nat: Internet service providers sometimes throttle connection speeds during peak streaming usage hours.

mis.bad: The server throttled down the network speed.
mis.good: The server throttled network requests / bandwidth.
mis.why: In software engineering, "throttle requests/bandwidth" is preferred without "down".

def: To prevent someone from accomplishing something, or stop an attempt from succeeding.
ex: Proactive security monitoring helped thwart several sophisticated phishing attempts targeting finance employees.
nat: Adverse winter weather conditions threatened to thwart our holiday travel plans completely.

mis.bad: The police thwarted against the robbery.
mis.good: The police thwarted the robbery attempt.
mis.why: "Thwart" is transitive; do not use the preposition "against".

def: Showing a lack of courage, confidence, or boldness; easily frightened.
ex: The new intern was rather timid and hesitated to speak during daily sprint standups.
nat: The frightened kitten took timid steps out of its cardboard carrier box.

mis.bad: He is very timid for speak.
mis.good: He is too timid to speak.
mis.why: Use "too timid to [verb]", not "timid for speak".

def: A trace of a color or quality, or a slight coloring.
ex: Her heartfelt speech carried a distinct tinge of melancholy as she said goodbye.
nat: The morning sky had a faint reddish tinge just before the sun rose.

mis.bad: The painting has an tinge of blue.
mis.good: The painting has a tinge of blue.
mis.why: The initial "t" is a consonant sound, so use the article "a".

def: A long, angry speech of criticism, accusation, or complaint.
ex: The frustrated customer launched into an angry tirade against the airport ticket agent.
nat: The manager delivered a furious tirade after discovering critical uncommitted production bugs.

mis.bad: He made a tirade about the service.
mis.good: He launched into a tirade about the service.
mis.why: The idiomatic verb collocation is "launch into a tirade".

pt: criança pequena / bebê que engatinha ou anda
def: A young child who is just beginning to walk, typically aged one to three.
ex: Watching an energetic toddler requires constant adult attention to prevent accidental household injuries.
nat: The neighborhood playground features a safe enclosed swing area specifically for toddlers.

mis.bad: She has a child toddler at home.
mis.good: She has a toddler at home.
mis.why: "Toddler" is already a noun for a young child; omit "child".

def: To work extremely hard and incessantly, especially doing strenuous physical labor.
ex: Farm workers had to toil under the blistering summer sun for ten hours daily.
nat: Software engineers toiled through the holiday weekend to resolve the database corruption.

mis.bad: He toiled on his desk until midnight.
mis.good: He toiled away at his desk until midnight.
mis.why: Use the idiom "toil away at [a task/desk]".

def: Showing willingness to allow the existence of opinions or behaviors one dislikes.
ex: Modern global software development teams thrive when team members remain tolerant of cultural differences.
nat: These desert plants are remarkably tolerant of extreme seasonal droughts and sandy soil.

mis.bad: He is very tolerant with other ideas.
mis.good: He is very tolerant of other ideas.
mis.why: The standard preposition after "tolerant" is "of", not "with".

def: A charge payable for using a bridge or road, or the cost in loss or suffering.
ex: Heavy overtime work and lack of sleep eventually took a severe toll on his health.
nat: Remember to keep small change ready for the highway toll booth ahead.

mis.bad: Stress made a toll on his body.
mis.good: Stress took a toll on his body.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "take a toll on", not "make a toll on".

def: Severe physical or mental suffering; a source of great pain.
ex: Waiting two agonizing weeks for medical biopsy test results was pure mental torment.
nat: Chronic back pain was a constant torment throughout his late retirement years.

mis.bad: He was in a big torment with the pain.
mis.good: He was in deep torment from the pain.
mis.why: Say "in deep torment", not "in a big torment".

def: A strong and fast-moving stream of water or other liquid, or overwhelming outpouring.
ex: The heavy tropical thunderstorm unleashed a violent torrent of muddy water down the hill.
nat: The announcement triggered a torrent of angry customer feedback across social media channels.

mis.bad: The rain fell with torrents.
mis.good: The rain fell in torrents / was pouring down.
mis.why: The correct phrase is "fell in torrents", not "with torrents".

def: The action or practice of inflicting severe pain as a punishment or coercion.
ex: Sitting through that four-hour unstructured committee meeting was absolute psychological torture for everyone.
nat: International human rights treaties strictly ban torture under all wartime or civil circumstances.

mis.bad: That meeting was a torture.
mis.good: That meeting was pure torture.
mis.why: In figurative English, "torture" is uncountable: say "pure torture" without "a".

def: Not explained or having the location or existence not known.
ex: The audit team discovered several unaccounted financial transactions dating back to the previous quarter.
nat: Three hikers remained unaccounted for after the sudden blizzard swept through the mountain pass.

mis.bad: Three workers are unaccounted from the factory.
mis.good: Three workers are unaccounted for from the factory.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "for" with the adjective phrase "unaccounted for".

def: Showing no prejudice for or against something; impartial.
ex: Machine learning engineers must audit training datasets to ensure algorithms produce fair and unbiased predictions.
nat: We hired an independent consulting agency to provide an unbiased evaluation of our infrastructure.

mis.bad: He gave an unbias review of the code.
mis.good: He gave an unbiased review of the code.
mis.why: Use the adjective form "unbiased" with "-ed", not "unbias".

def: Strange or mysterious, especially in an unsettling way; beyond normal human expectation.
ex: The generative language model demonstrated an uncanny ability to mimic the author distinctive voice.
nat: There was an uncanny resemblance between the two distant cousins who had never met.

mis.bad: She has an uncanny to predict market trends.
mis.good: She has an uncanny ability to predict market trends.
mis.why: "Uncanny" is an adjective; combine with a noun like "uncanny ability".

def: To estimate something to be smaller or less important than it really is.
ex: Never underestimate the amount of time needed to migrate legacy production databases without downtime.
nat: The marketing department underestimated customer demand for the newly announced smart home gadget.

mis.bad: Do not under estimate the competitor.
mis.good: Do not underestimate the competitor.
mis.why: Write "underestimate" as a single unified word without space.

def: Significant as a cause or basis of something, but not necessarily obvious.
ex: The team conducted a thorough root cause analysis to identify the underlying database failure.
nat: Stress and lack of quality sleep were the underlying reasons for her chronic fatigue.

mis.bad: We need to solve the underline problem.
mis.good: We need to solve the underlying problem.
mis.why: Use "underlying" (adjective), not "underline" (verb/noun).

def: To commit oneself to and begin an enterprise, responsibility, or journey.
ex: The engineering team agreed to undertake a major rewrite of the legacy frontend codebase.
nat: She undertook full responsibility for coordinating customer onboarding during the product rollout.

mis.bad: He undertook to doing the audit alone.
mis.good: He undertook to do the audit alone.
mis.why: Use "undertake to + base verb", not "-ing".

def: To sign and accept liability under an insurance policy or guarantee a financial issuance.
ex: Several leading investment banks agreed to underwrite the technology firm upcoming initial public offering.
nat: Insurance companies carefully assess coastal property risk before agreeing to underwrite home policies.

mis.bad: The bank underwrited the debt.
mis.good: The bank underwrote the debt.
mis.why: Irregular past tense: underwrite — underwrote — underwritten.

def: Unwarranted or inappropriate because excessive or disproportionate.
ex: Aggressive project deadlines can place undue stress on software development teams and lead to burnout.
nat: The board took precautions to prevent the founding investor from exercising undue influence over decisions.

mis.bad: Do not put an undue pressure on him.
mis.good: Do not put undue pressure on him.
mis.why: "Pressure" is uncountable here; say "undue pressure" without "an".

def: Not disconcerted or perturbed by unexpected difficulties or criticism.
ex: The veteran conference speaker remained completely unfazed when the presentation projector suddenly lost power.
nat: She was unfazed by the hostile questions posed by skeptical financial journalists during the briefing.

mis.bad: He was unfaced by the bad news.
mis.good: He was unfazed by the bad news.
mis.why: Spell "unfazed" with "z", meaning undisturbed (not related to "face").

def: To open or spread out from a folded state, or develop over time.
ex: News channels broadcast live updates as dramatic political events began to unfold across the capital.
nat: The tourist unfolded the paper subway map to find the correct interchange train station.

mis.bad: We watched the situation unfolding down.
mis.good: We watched the situation unfold.
mis.why: Do not add "down"; simply use "unfold" for events developing.

def: The quality or state of being uniform, homogenous, or identical throughout.
ex: Adopting a shared style guide ensures visual uniformity across all enterprise customer portal screens.
nat: Industrial automation guarantees complete uniformity in product packaging dimensions and weight.

mis.bad: There is no uniformness in the process.
mis.good: There is no uniformity in the process.
mis.why: Use the correct noun "uniformity", not "uniformness".

pt: unilateral / tomado por apenas um lado
def: Action or decision performed by or affecting only one person, group, or country.
ex: The CEO unilateral decision to cancel remote work policies sparked immediate employee dissatisfaction and resignations.
nat: The neighboring nation declared a unilateral ceasefire ahead of international diplomatic peace negotiations.

mis.bad: It was an unilateral action by the boss.
mis.good: It was a unilateral action by the boss.
mis.why: "Unilateral" begins with the /j/ consonant sound, so use the article "a".

def: Impossible to understand or comprehend due to poor audio or unclear expression.
ex: The voice message was completely unintelligible because of poor cellular reception during the storm.
nat: The handwritten doctor prescription was virtually unintelligible to the pharmacy technician.

mis.bad: His speech was unintelligible to understand.
mis.good: His speech was unintelligible.
mis.why: Avoid the redundant "to understand" after "unintelligible".

def: To release something powerful, violent, or previously restrained.
ex: The breakthrough artificial intelligence model will unleash unprecedented creative productivity across multiple knowledge industries.
nat: Heavy tropical storms threatened to unleash catastrophic flash floods throughout the river valley.

mis.bad: The update unleashed out new bugs.
mis.good: The update unleashed new bugs.
mis.why: Do not add "out"; "unleash" takes a direct object without prepositions.

def: Not able to be mistaken for anything else; very distinctive.
ex: The signature aroma of freshly roasted espresso coffee is unmistakable whenever you enter the cafe.
nat: There was an unmistakable look of relief on his face when the test passed.

mis.bad: Her voice has an unmistakable sound of Brazilian.
mis.good: Her voice has an unmistakable Brazilian accent.
mis.why: Use "unmistakable [nationality] accent", not "sound of [nationality]".

def: To investigate and solve a mystery, or gradually fall apart or collapse.
ex: Data scientists worked diligently to unravel the complex patterns hidden inside consumer purchasing records.
nat: The corporate merger agreement began to unravel over unresolved executive leadership disagreements.

mis.bad: The conspiracy began to unravel down.
mis.good: The conspiracy began to unravel.
mis.why: Omit "down"; "unravel" is complete on its own.

def: Not yielding in strength, severity, or determination; constant and fierce.
ex: The startup achieved remarkable product market fit through unrelenting focus on direct customer feedback.
nat: Firefighters battled against unrelenting desert winds while containing the fast-moving mountain wildfire.

mis.bad: He worked with an unrelenting dedication.
mis.good: He worked with unrelenting dedication.
mis.why: "Dedication" is uncountable here; say "with unrelenting dedication" without "an".

def: Disorderly and disruptive and not amenable to discipline or control.
ex: Flight attendants had to restrain an unruly passenger who refused to wear his seatbelt.
nat: Humidity always makes her naturally curly hair unruly and difficult to style in mornings.

mis.bad: The children were very unruled in class.
mis.good: The children were very unruly in class.
mis.why: Use the established adjective "unruly", not "unruled".

def: Having or showing no moral principles; not honest or fair.
ex: Unscrupulous telemarketers often target elderly individuals with fraudulent health supplement subscription schemes.
nat: The audit uncovered unscrupulous billing practices designed to inflate billable consulting hours artificially.

mis.bad: He is an unscrupulous businessman without morals.
mis.good: He is an unscrupulous businessman.
mis.why: "Unscrupulous" already implies lack of morals; avoid adding "without morals".

def: Given or done voluntarily, without having been asked for or requested.
ex: Our company email spam filters automatically quarantine unsolicited sales pitches and promotional newsletters.
nat: She gave me unsolicited advice about my career choices while having coffee together.

mis.bad: I received many unsolicited advices.
mis.good: I received a lot of unsolicited advice.
mis.why: "Advice" is strictly uncountable in English; never add "-s" to advice.

def: To make something free from tangles, or resolve a complicated situation.
ex: It took senior engineers several days to untangle the spaghetti code in the legacy module.
nat: She sat patiently on the floor trying to untangle the colorful holiday string lights.

mis.bad: I untangled the cables of the floor.
mis.good: I untangled the cables on the floor.
mis.why: Use "cables on the floor", not "of".

def: To show or introduce a new product, plan, or artwork to the public.
ex: The automaker plans to unveil its next-generation electric sports sedan at the Geneva auto show.
nat: The mayor will unveil the newly restored bronze monument in the central city square.

mis.bad: They unveiled up the new design today.
mis.good: They unveiled the new design today.
mis.why: Do not add "up" to "unveil"; it takes a direct object.

def: Not justified or authorized; lacking proper basis or necessity.
ex: Her harsh criticism of the intern presentation was completely unwarranted and frankly unprofessional.
nat: The market sharp drop was an unwarranted overreaction to brief temporary supply disruptions.

mis.bad: That comment was unwarranted of reason.
mis.good: That comment was unwarranted and unfair.
mis.why: Use "unwarranted" without "of reason", as it already means without justification.

def: Without being aware; unintentionally or unknowingly.
ex: By downloading the pirated software utility, he unwittingly exposed his computer to malicious malware.
nat: She unwittingly revealed the surprise party plans during a casual family phone call.

mis.bad: He made that mistake unwittingly of the consequences.
mis.good: He made that mistake unwittingly, without realizing the consequences.
mis.why: "Unwittingly" is an adverb and does not take "of".

def: Cheerful, enthusiastic, and optimistic in tone or attitude.
ex: Despite the challenging economic climate, the company quarterly earnings call struck an upbeat tone.
nat: She remained upbeat and cheerful throughout the long and exhausting international travel flight.

mis.bad: He gave an upbeat news about the project.
mis.good: He gave upbeat news / an upbeat update about the project.
mis.why: "News" is uncountable; say "upbeat news" without "an".

def: To waver between different opinions or actions; be indecisive.
ex: The committee members continued to vacillate between hiring an external consultant or promoting internally.
nat: Do not vacillate when making critical emergency production rollback decisions during deployment failures.

mis.bad: He vacillated of opinion many times.
mis.good: He vacillated between opinions / kept vacillating.
mis.why: Use "vacillate between [options]", not "of".

def: Possessing or showing courage or determination in the face of danger.
ex: Despite their valiant defensive efforts, the local football team lost the championship match.
nat: Firefighters made a valiant attempt to rescue residents trapped inside the burning apartment.

mis.bad: They did an effort valiant to win.
mis.good: They made a valiant effort to win.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a valiant effort".

def: To disappear suddenly and completely from sight or existence.
ex: The morning ocean fog began to vanish quickly once the bright sun rose overhead.
nat: All our preliminary code draft notes vanished when the unsaved laptop battery died.

mis.bad: My keys vanished down from the table.
mis.good: My keys vanished into thin air / disappeared.
mis.why: Do not say "vanished down"; use "vanished into thin air" or "vanished".

def: Excessive pride in or admiration of one's own appearance or achievements.
ex: His relentless self-promotion on professional networks seemed driven more by personal vanity than merit.
nat: The master bathroom features a modern double vanity sink with elegant marble countertops.

mis.bad: She has a lot of vanities.
mis.good: She has a lot of vanity / is very vain.
mis.why: As a personality trait, "vanity" is uncountable.

def: A group of people leading the way in new developments or ideas.
ex: Our engineering research lab aims to remain at the vanguard of artificial intelligence innovations.
nat: Independent artists were in the vanguard of the modern cultural renaissance in Berlin.

mis.bad: The company is on the vanguard of technology.
mis.good: The company is at the vanguard of technology.
mis.why: Use the preposition "at the vanguard of", not "on".

def: To defeat thoroughly in a battle, contest, or competition.
ex: The defending grandmaster managed to vanquish his young challenger in thirty-two precise chess moves.
nat: Courage and disciplined daily study will help you vanquish your fear of public speaking.

mis.bad: He vanquished with all his rivals.
mis.good: He vanquished all his rivals.
mis.why: "Vanquish" is transitive and takes a direct object without "with".

def: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging; dull and uninteresting.
ex: Critics dismissed the reality television program as a vapid collection of scripted drama.
nat: The panel discussion suffered from vapid platitudes instead of concrete technical solutions.

mis.bad: The talk was very vapid to listen.
mis.good: The talk was vapid and boring to listen to.
mis.why: Use "vapid" on its own or pair with "dull/boring".

def: A form or version of something that differs in some respect from others.
ex: Health officials monitored the emergence of a new genetic variant of the respiratory virus.
nat: The automotive company released a turbocharged hybrid variant of its popular family sedan.

mis.bad: This is an variant more fast.
mis.good: This is a faster variant.
mis.why: Place the comparative adjective before the noun: "a faster variant".

def: A change or difference in condition, amount, or level, typically within limits.
ex: Regional temperature variation can significantly impact battery performance in cold outdoor electric fleet vehicles.
nat: There is considerable regional variation in how Brazilian Portuguese slang is spoken nationwide.

mis.bad: There are many variation of this recipe.
mis.good: There are many variations of this recipe.
mis.why: Use the plural "variations" with "many".

def: To change direction suddenly or unexpectedly, especially a moving vehicle or discussion.
ex: The driver had to veer sharply to the left to avoid hitting a deer.
nat: The casual conversation began to veer toward contentious political issues during the team dinner.

mis.bad: The car veered from the road to right.
mis.good: The car veered sharply to the right.
mis.why: Use "veer to the right/left" or "veer off the road".

def: Showing strong feeling; forceful, passionate, or intense.
ex: The opposition party issued a vehement denial regarding allegations of electoral campaign misconduct.
nat: She gave a vehement defense of consumer privacy rights during the congressional technology hearing.

mis.bad: He was very vehement with his words.
mis.good: He was vehement in his speech / spoke vehemently.
mis.why: Use "vehement in [something]" or the adverb "vehemently".

def: Expressed in an indirect way; not openly declared or revealed.
ex: His diplomatic opening remarks contained a thinly veiled threat about future bilateral trade tariffs.
nat: She sent a politely veiled message indicating that the partnership contract was ending.

mis.bad: It was a criticism veiled to the manager.
mis.good: It was a veiled criticism of the manager.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a veiled criticism".

def: The speed of something in a given direction, or rapidity of motion.
ex: Scrum masters track sprint velocity to estimate how many story points teams deliver biweekly.
nat: The rocket achieved orbital velocity just eight minutes after launching from the pad.

mis.bad: What is the velocity of this car?
mis.good: What is the speed of this car?
mis.why: In everyday English, use "speed"; "velocity" is technical or directional (physics/agile).

def: Accorded a great deal of respect, especially because of age, wisdom, or character.
ex: The venerable university law library houses centuries of rare historical legal manuscripts and treaties.
nat: The company was founded over a century ago by a venerable industrial innovator.

mis.bad: He is an venerable doctor of our city.
mis.good: He is a venerable doctor in our city.
mis.why: Use "in our city", not "of our city".

def: To regard with great respect; revere.
ex: Many indigenous cultures deeply venerate ancient natural forests as sacred ancestral living spirits.
nat: Software developers around the world venerate pioneer computer scientists who created open-source operating systems.

mis.bad: They venerate to the old masters.
mis.good: They venerate the old masters.
mis.why: "Venerate" takes a direct object without the preposition "to".

def: Punishment inflicted or retribution exacted for an injury, wrong, or grievance.
ex: He spent years plotting legal vengeance against the corrupt partners who ruined his business.
nat: After a slow start in the first half, the home team scored with a vengeance.

mis.bad: He took a vengeance on his enemy.
mis.good: He took vengeance on his enemy.
mis.why: "Vengeance" is uncountable; say "took vengeance on" without "a".

def: Conformity to facts; accuracy, truthfulness, or correctness.
ex: Cybersecurity investigators carefully checked the veracity of the leaked customer database dump credentials.
nat: Independent journalists questioned the veracity of the official government statistics on unemployment rates.

mis.bad: I have doubts about the veracity from this news.
mis.good: I have doubts about the veracity of this news.
mis.why: Use the preposition "of", not "from": "veracity of this news".

pt: literalmente / palavra por palavra / ipsis litteris
def: In exactly the same words as were used originally.
ex: The court stenographer transcribed the witness testimony verbatim during the high-profile criminal trial.
nat: You should not copy text verbatim from Wikipedia into your final academic research paper.

mis.bad: She memorized the poem in verbatim.
mis.good: She memorized the poem verbatim.
mis.why: Do not use "in" before "verbatim"; it functions directly as an adverb or adjective.

def: Using or expressed in more words than are needed; wordy.
ex: Set the application logging configuration to verbose mode to diagnose intermittent connection errors.
nat: His executive summary was too verbose and buried the main recommendations under excessive technical jargon.

mis.bad: His code comments are very verboses.
mis.good: His code comments are very verbose.
mis.why: English adjectives never take a plural "-s".

def: Bright green with lush, thriving plant life and vegetation.
ex: The narrow train wound through verdant terraced valleys in the coffee-growing highlands.
nat: Spring rains transformed the dry countryside into a verdant landscape of wildflower meadows.

mis.bad: The hills are very verdant of trees.
mis.good: The hills are lush and verdant with trees.
mis.why: Use "with", not "of": "verdant with vegetation".

def: An edge or border, or an extreme limit beyond which something occurs.
ex: The exhausted startup founders were on the verge of giving up before securing investment.
nat: Spring wild flowers bloomed profusely along the grassy road verge outside the village.

mis.bad: She was in the verge of tears.
mis.good: She was on the verge of tears.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "on the verge of", not "in".

def: Able to be checked or demonstrated to be true, accurate, or justified.
ex: Scientific conclusions must always rely on verifiable empirical experimental data collected under controlled conditions.
nat: Candidates must provide verifiable employment references before a formal job offer is issued.

mis.bad: We need proofs verifiables for this claim.
mis.good: We need verifiable proof for this claim.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "verifiable proof".

def: The ability to adapt or be adapted to many different functions or activities.
ex: Engineers admire Python programming language versatility for building both web backends and machine learning.
nat: Her impressive versatility as an actor allows her to play both drama and comedy.

mis.bad: The tool has a lot of versatile.
mis.good: The tool has great versatility / is very versatile.
mis.why: Use the noun "versatility" after have, not the adjective "versatile".

def: Writing arranged with a metrical rhythm, typically having a rhyme scheme.
ex: The famous English poet wrote beautiful romantic verse inspired by the countryside landscape.
nat: Let us sing the second verse of the traditional holiday song together now.

mis.bad: He wrote a poem with four verses.
mis.good: He wrote a poem with four stanzas / verses.
mis.why: In a song or hymn, each section is a "verse"; in poetry, each section is usually a "stanza".

def: At right angles to a horizontal plane; pointing straight up and down.
ex: The modern luxury office tower features an innovative vertical garden climbing its glass facade.
nat: Maintain a vertical posture with your shoulders back to avoid chronic spinal strain.

mis.bad: Draw a line vertical on the paper.
mis.good: Draw a vertical line on the paper.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a vertical line".

pt: andar na água rasa / avançar com dificuldade
def: To walk through water or other liquid with effort, or laboriously sift data.
ex: We had to wade through knee-deep river water to reach the hidden campsite.
nat: The compliance auditor had to wade through hundreds of legacy financial accounting spreadsheets.

mis.bad: We waded on the river water.
mis.good: We waded through the river water.
mis.why: Use the preposition "through" with wade: "wade through water".

def: To speak or write at length in a vague, rambling, or indecisive manner.
ex: The politician began to waffle when reporters pressed him on specific tax reform details.
nat: Please get straight to the point in your executive summary instead of waffling.

mis.bad: He waffled about the question for ten minutes.
mis.good: He waffled on the question for ten minutes.
mis.why: In British and Commonwealth usage, you "waffle on" about a subject.

def: To risk a sum of money or valuable item against someone on an outcome.
ex: I would wager that our new payment checkout design will double mobile conversion rates.
nat: He decided to wager fifty dollars on the horse with the highest odds.

mis.bad: I wager in that he will win.
mis.good: I would wager that he will win / I bet that he will win.
mis.why: Use "wager that [clause]", omitting "in".

pt: abrir mão de / dispensar / renunciar a
def: To refrain from insisting on or using a legal right, fee, or claim.
ex: The university agreed to waive the application fee for international students from developing countries.
nat: By signing the sports liability form, you waive your right to pursue legal damages.

mis.bad: They waived from the late fee.
mis.good: They waived the late fee.
mis.why: "Waive" is transitive and takes a direct object without "from".

def: An act or instance of waiving a right or claim, or document stating this.
ex: All participants must sign a liability waiver before taking part in the skydiving tour.
nat: The bank granted a temporary waiver on monthly overdraft charges during economic recovery.

mis.bad: I signed an waiver for the excursion.
mis.good: I signed a waiver for the excursion.
mis.why: Pronounce "waiver" starting with /w/, so use the indefinite article "a".

def: To have a progressively smaller part of the visible surface illuminated, or decrease.
ex: Public enthusiasm for the new virtual reality headset began to wane after several months.
nat: The bright full moon will gradually wane over the next two weeks at night.

mis.bad: His interest was in the wane.
mis.good: His interest was on the wane.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "on the wane", not "in the wane".

def: A separate room or division in a hospital, or an administrative electoral district.
ex: The patient was transferred from intensive care to the orthopedic recovery ward this morning.
nat: Local candidates campaigned door to door across every residential ward in the metropolitan area.

mis.bad: She works in the ward of pediatric.
mis.good: She works in the pediatric ward.
mis.why: Put the adjective before the noun: "pediatric ward".

def: To make or become bent or twisted out of shape, typically from heat or damp.
ex: Excessive bathroom moisture will warp the unsealed wooden floorboards over several winter months.
nat: Extreme political bias can warp someone perception of objective economic and scientific facts.

mis.bad: The wood warped down from the rain.
mis.good: The wood warped from the rain.
mis.why: Do not say "warped down"; use "warped from moisture".

def: Feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems; suspicious.
ex: Consumers are increasingly wary of entering personal credit card numbers on unfamiliar online stores.
nat: The stray cat was wary of humans and would not approach the food bowl.

mis.bad: Be wary with that email link.
mis.good: Be wary of that email link.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "of" after "wary", not "with".

def: To shake with a quivering motion, or become unsteady or indecisive.
ex: Her commitment to completing the difficult marathon never wavered despite painful leg muscle cramps.
nat: The candlelight began to waver gently as a cool draft entered through the window.

mis.bad: He wavered in his decision to leave.
mis.good: He wavered in his decision to leave.
mis.why: Do not confuse "waver" (hesitate) with "waiver" (document giving up a right).

def: Feeling or showing tiredness, especially as a result of excessive exertion or lack.
ex: The weary travelers collapsed gratefully into comfortable hotel beds after a twenty-hour international flight.
nat: Citizens grew weary of hearing the same empty political campaign promises year after year.

mis.bad: I am weary with this noise.
mis.good: I am weary of this noise.
mis.why: Use the preposition "of" when meaning tired or sick of something: "weary of".

def: A piece of wood, metal, or food having one thick end tapering to a thin edge.
ex: The server brought a fresh wedge of sharp cheddar cheese alongside the fruit platter.
nat: He used a small wooden wedge to prop the heavy fire door securely open.

mis.bad: Add a lemon wedge on the glass.
mis.good: Add a lemon wedge to the glass.
mis.why: Say "add a wedge of lemon to the drink".

def: To shed tears, typically as an expression of grief, sorrow, or deep emotion.
ex: She could not help but weep tears of joy when her long-lost brother arrived.
nat: The tragic novel made readers weep openly during the poignant final three chapters.

mis.bad: She weeped when she heard the news.
mis.good: She wept when she heard the news.
mis.why: Irregular past tense: weep — wept — wept (not "weeped").

def: Weighing a great deal; of great seriousness and importance.
ex: The executive committee met to debate weighty strategic questions about future international expansion plans.
nat: The legal judge carried a weighty stack of case files into the courtroom chamber.

mis.bad: This is a weighty problem for solve.
mis.good: This is a weighty problem to solve.
mis.why: Use "to solve", not "for solve".

def: Suggesting something supernatural; strikingly odd, unusual, or strange.
ex: I heard a weird buzzing noise coming from the computer power supply unit yesterday.
nat: It felt weird returning to my quiet hometown after living in Tokyo for five years.

mis.bad: That sound is very weirdly.
mis.good: That sound is very weird.
mis.why: Use the adjective "weird" after linking verbs like "is" or "sounds".

def: A sudden desire or change of mind, especially one that is unusual or unexplained.
ex: On a sudden whim, they bought tickets to Paris and flew out that evening.
nat: Do not make important career or financial decisions purely on an impulsive whim.

mis.bad: We traveled by a whim.
mis.good: We traveled on a whim.
mis.why: The correct idiomatic preposition is "on a whim", not "by".

def: Playfully quaint or fanciful, especially in an appealing and amusing way.
ex: The children storybook features delightful, whimsical illustrations of talking animals wearing colorful woolen hats.
nat: Her quirky, whimsical sense of humor always brightens up otherwise dull engineering standup meetings.

mis.bad: The design has a style very whimsical.
mis.good: The design has a very whimsical style.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a very whimsical style".

def: A column of rapidly rotating air, or a tumultuous and rapidly changing event.
ex: The startup team went on a whirlwind promotional tour visiting six cities in eight days.
nat: A sudden dusty whirlwind kicked up dry leaves across the open parking lot.

mis.bad: They had a romance of whirlwind.
mis.good: They had a whirlwind romance.
mis.why: Use "whirlwind romance" as a compound noun phrase.

def: Conducive to or promoting moral or physical well-being; healthy and pure.
ex: The farm-to-table restaurant serves wholesome homemade meals prepared with organic seasonal regional ingredients.
nat: Spending quality time outdoors with family provides wholesome entertainment away from digital screens.

mis.bad: This soup is very wholesome for the health.
mis.good: This soup is wholesome and healthy.
mis.why: Say "wholesome", which already means good for health; omit "for the health".

def: To hold and use a weapon, or exert power, authority, or influence effectively.
ex: Senior tech executives wield immense influence over global internet communication standards and consumer privacy.
nat: The ancient warrior was trained to wield a heavy steel broadsword with one hand.

mis.bad: He wields of great power in the company.
mis.good: He wields great power in the company.
mis.why: "Wield" is transitive and takes a direct object without "of".

def: Done intentionally and deliberately, or stubborn and determined to have one's own way.
ex: The auditor cited repeated willful violations of environmental and employee workplace safety regulations.
nat: The willful toddler refused to wear a jacket despite the freezing cold morning wind.

mis.bad: It was an willful act of sabotage.
mis.good: It was a willful act of sabotage.
mis.why: "Willful" begins with the consonant sound /w/, so use the article "a".

def: To make a grimacing movement because of pain, distress, or embarrassment.
ex: He could not help but wince when the dentist touched the sensitive cracked tooth.
nat: I had to wince when reading the embarrassing typos in the printed wedding invitation.

mis.bad: He winced of pain when he fell.
mis.good: He winced in pain when he fell.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "wince in pain", not "of pain".

def: A piece of unexpected good fortune, typically involving receiving a large amount of money.
ex: The unexpected inheritance gave the young family a financial windfall to clear their debts.
nat: The energy company paid a special windfall tax on record quarterly international export profits.

mis.bad: They received a windfall of money.
mis.good: They received a financial windfall.
mis.why: "Windfall" already implies money or fortune; use "financial windfall".

def: Showing quick and inventive verbal humor; amusingly clever.
ex: Her witty commentary during the conference panel discussion kept the entire audience engaged throughout.
nat: Oscar Wilde is famous for his sharp and witty epigrams about Victorian society.

mis.bad: He made an comment very witty.
mis.good: He made a very witty comment.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a very witty comment".

def: To move unsteadily from side to side, or waver in confidence.
ex: The cheap wooden dining chair began to wobble whenever someone sat down on it.
nat: Investor confidence began to wobble as inflation figures exceeded initial government forecasts this morning.

mis.bad: The table wobbles down because of the leg.
mis.good: The table wobbles because of the uneven leg.
mis.why: Do not say "wobbles down"; simply say "wobbles".

def: Great sorrow or distress; or trouble and problems in plural form.
ex: Supply chain disruptions added to the economic woes facing the domestic automotive manufacturing sector.
nat: She listened with compassion as her friend shared personal woes about his difficult divorce.

mis.bad: The country has many woes economic.
mis.good: The country has many economic woes.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "economic woes".

def: To have a long, complicated, and heated dispute, or manage difficult data.
ex: Attorneys for both companies spent weeks attempting to wrangle over intellectual property licensing terms.
nat: Data engineers spend significant daily hours wrangling messy data into clean, structured analytics tables.

mis.bad: They wrangled about of the contract details.
mis.good: They wrangled over the contract details.
mis.why: The standard collocation is "wrangle over [an issue]".

def: An arrangement of flowers, leaves, or stems fastened in a circular ring.
ex: Dignitaries placed a memorial wreath of red poppies at the national tomb of veterans.
nat: She hung a festive evergreen pine wreath on her front door for Christmas.

mis.bad: They putted a wreath on the grave.
mis.good: They laid a wreath on the grave / put a wreath on the grave.
mis.why: Past tense of "put" is "put", not "putted", and the traditional formal verb is "lay".

def: To destroy or severely damage a vehicle, building, or someone's plans.
ex: The severe winter thunderstorm threatened to wreck our planned weekend camping trip to mountains.
nat: A careless distracted driver managed to completely wreck his new luxury sports utility vehicle.

mis.bad: He wrecked with his car on the highway.
mis.good: He wrecked his car on the highway.
mis.why: "Wreck" is transitive and takes a direct object without "with".

pt: torcer / arrancar com força / ferir emocionalmente
def: To pull, twist, or turn someone or something violently away.
ex: He managed to wrench the rusted metal bolt loose using a heavy adjustable spanner.
nat: Leaving her childhood hometown for an overseas job was an emotionally wrenching life decision.

mis.bad: He wrenched the door of the frame.
mis.good: He wrenched the door from the frame.
mis.why: Use "from", not "of": "wrenched from the frame".

def: In a very unhappy or unfortunate state; of very poor quality or condition.
ex: The homeless family endured wretched living conditions in an abandoned warehouse during winter months.
nat: I felt wretched with a high fever and migraine headache for three days straight.

mis.bad: He lives in a condition wretched.
mis.good: He lives in wretched conditions.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "wretched conditions".

def: Using or expressing dry, especially mocking or sarcastic, humor.
ex: She gave a wry smile when she heard that the delayed train was canceled.
nat: The author sharp, wry observations about corporate office life made the novel hilarious.

mis.bad: He looked with an wry expression.
mis.good: He looked with a wry expression.
mis.why: The initial /r/ sound is a consonant sound, so use the article "a".

def: To make or become wider, or expand the scope of knowledge or operations.
ex: The municipal government decided to widen the suburban highway from two to four lanes.
nat: Reading international newspapers in English will quickly widen your active vocabulary and worldview.

mis.bad: We need to broad our market.
mis.good: We need to widen our market / broaden our reach.
mis.why: "Broad" is an adjective; use the verb "widen" or "broaden".

pt: reter / reter informações / recusar-se a dar
def: To refuse to give something that is due to or desired by someone.
ex: The investigation committee accused the executive of attempting to withhold critical internal audit documents.
nat: Employers must withhold federal income tax directly from employees monthly salary paychecks by law.

mis.bad: Do not withhold with the truth.
mis.good: Do not withhold the truth.
mis.why: "Withhold" is transitive and takes a direct object without "with".

def: Worth the time, money, or effort spent; valuable or rewarding.
ex: Investing thirty minutes each morning in English speaking practice is an exceptionally worthwhile habit.
nat: Volunteering at the local animal shelter proved to be a deeply worthwhile personal experience.

mis.bad: It is worth while to do it.
mis.good: It is worthwhile to do it / worth doing it.
mis.why: Write "worthwhile" as a single compound adjective.

def: To have an intense feeling of longing for something, typically something unobtainable.
ex: After five years living abroad, he began to yearn for the warm tropical beaches.
nat: Exhausted healthcare workers yearned for a brief period of uninterrupted rest and recovery.

mis.bad: I yearn of seeing my family.
mis.good: I yearn to see my family / yearn for my family.
mis.why: Use "yearn for [noun]" or "yearn to + base verb", not "of".

pt: critério de medição / padrão de comparação
def: A standard, measurement, or criterion against which other things are judged or compared.
ex: Customer retention rate is the primary yardstick by which our subscription startup measures success.
nat: Examination scores should not be the sole yardstick used to assess student intellectual creativity.

mis.bad: Exam scores are not the only yard-stick.
mis.good: Exam scores are not the only yardstick.
mis.why: Write "yardstick" as a single unified noun without a hyphen.

pt: ganir / dar um ganido / gritar de dor
def: To give a short, sharp, and high-pitched cry of pain or alarm.
ex: The small puppy gave a loud yelp when I accidentally stepped on its paw.
nat: He let out an involuntary yelp when he touched the hot oven rack.

mis.bad: The dog gave an yelp of fear.
mis.good: The dog let out a yelp of pain.
mis.why: Use the verb phrase "let out a yelp" with the indefinite article "a".

def: A wooden crosspiece fastened over draft animals, or a symbol of heavy oppression.
ex: The rebellious colony fought a bitter war to throw off the foreign imperial yoke.
nat: Oxen pulled the wooden plow together under a sturdy hand-carved oak timber yoke.

mis.bad: Do not confuse the egg yolk with this yoke.
mis.good: Do not confuse the egg yolk (/joʊk/) with the wooden yoke (/joʊk/).
mis.why: Note that "yolk" (egg yellow) and "yoke" (harness/oppression) are homophones.

def: At some distance in the direction indicated; over there; more distant.
ex: Look at the snowy mountain peaks visible beyond yonder green pine ridge in distance.
nat: The shepherd guided his sheep toward yonder meadow on the far hillside slope.

mis.bad: Look at the house over yonder there.
mis.good: Look at the house over yonder.
mis.why: "Over yonder" already means "over there"; do not add "there" redundantly.

def: Remaining young, or having the vitality, enthusiasm, and appearance characteristic of youth.
ex: Regular cardiovascular physical exercise and adequate sleep help you maintain a youthful healthy glow.
nat: The team leader contagious youthful enthusiasm inspired everyone during the challenging hackathon weekend.

mis.bad: She has an appearance very youthful.
mis.good: She has a very youthful appearance.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a very youthful appearance".

def: A well-paid young middle-class professional who works in a city.
ex: Gentrification transformed the old warehouse district into a trendy neighborhood populated by affluent yuppies.
nat: The chic cafe serves specialty avocado toast and matcha latte to neighborhood yuppies.

mis.bad: He became an yuppie after moving to New York.
mis.good: He became a yuppie after moving to New York.
mis.why: The initial "y" is a consonant sound /j/, so use "a yuppie".

def: To involuntarily open one's mouth wide and inhale deeply due to tiredness.
ex: Try to cover your mouth politely with your hand whenever you feel like yawning.
nat: The sleepy student tried not to yawn while the teacher explained mathematical equations.

mis.bad: I made a big yawn during the lecture.
mis.good: I yawned / let out a big yawn during the lecture.
mis.why: Use the verb "yawn" or "let out a yawn", not "made a yawn".

def: A child, young person, or youth, typically an adolescent.
ex: The community sports center organizes weekend basketball leagues for energetic local neighborhood youngsters.
nat: A polite youngster helped the elderly woman carry heavy grocery bags up stairs.

mis.bad: There were many youngs in the park.
mis.good: There were many youngsters in the park.
mis.why: Do not say "youngs"; use "youngsters" or "young people".

def: The yellow internal part of a bird egg, rich in protein and fat.
ex: Gently separate the egg yolk from the clear egg white before whipping them.
nat: I love dipping crispy buttered sourdough toast into a runny soft-boiled egg yolk.

mis.bad: I ate the yellow of the egg.
mis.good: I ate the egg yolk.
mis.why: In English, use "egg yolk" rather than literal "the yellow of the egg".

def: Great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause, objective, or belief.
ex: The new software developer tackled legacy refactoring tasks with remarkable energy and enthusiastic zeal.
nat: Her missionary zeal for animal rescue inspired dozens of volunteers to join shelters.

mis.bad: He worked with a big zeal.
mis.good: He worked with great zeal / enthusiasm.
mis.why: Say "with great zeal", avoiding "a big zeal".

def: A person who is fanatical and uncompromising in pursuit of religious or political ideals.
ex: The technology architect was an open-source zealot who refused to use proprietary operating systems.
nat: Political zealots often refuse to compromise or consider valid perspectives from opposing viewpoints.

mis.bad: He is an zealot of Linux.
mis.good: He is a Linux zealot.
mis.why: Use the noun adjunct: "a Linux zealot" or "a zealot for Linux".

def: Having or showing zeal; passionate and fiercely devoted to a cause.
ex: The company compliance department was remarkably zealous in enforcing international trade sanction rules.
nat: He was a zealous advocate for clean renewable solar energy across the state.

mis.bad: He is very zealous of his privacy.
mis.good: He is very zealous about his privacy / protective of his privacy.
mis.why: Use "zealous about [a topic]" rather than "zealous of".

def: The time at which something is most powerful, successful, or at its highest.
ex: The ancient empire reached the zenith of its global economic power during the second century.
nat: The midday summer sun reached its zenith directly overhead in the cloudless blue sky.

mis.bad: The business is on the zenith of success.
mis.good: The business is at the zenith of success.
mis.why: The correct preposition is "at the zenith of", not "on".

pt: raspa de fruta cítrica / entusiasmo / ânimo
def: Great enthusiasm and energy, or the outer colored part of citrus peel.
ex: Grate the fresh lemon zest finely over the warm pasta before serving the meal.
nat: She has a remarkable zest for life that inspires everyone around her daily.

mis.bad: Add some scrapes of lemon on the cake.
mis.good: Add some lemon zest to the cake.
mis.why: In culinary English, use "lemon zest", not "scrapes of lemon".

def: To move along a path that has a series of short, sharp turns.
ex: The scenic mountain hiking trail began to zigzag steeply up the rocky canyon face.
nat: The frightened rabbit zigzags rapidly across the open meadow to escape the hungry hawk.

mis.bad: The car made zigzags on the road.
mis.good: The car zigzagged down the road.
mis.why: Use the verb "zigzagged", rather than "made zigzags".

def: A device consisting of two flexible strips of metal or plastic with interlocking teeth.
ex: The metal zipper on my winter coat got stuck on the pocket fabric yesterday.
nat: Make sure the zipper on your travel backpack is completely closed in crowded stations.

mis.bad: The fecho of my jacket broke.
mis.good: The zipper on my jacket broke.
mis.why: Use the English word "zipper", not Portuguese "fecho".

def: A belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, used in astrological horoscopes.
ex: She asked what my astrological zodiac sign was during our first casual lunch date.
nat: The ancient Greek astronomical chart illustrates the twelve classical constellations of the zodiac.

mis.bad: What is your sign of zodiac?
mis.good: What is your zodiac sign?
mis.why: Use the compound noun phrase "zodiac sign".

def: A corpse said to be revived, or a computer controlled by another machine.
ex: The DevOps engineer discovered several zombie processes consuming valuable server memory in the background.
nat: I felt like a mindless zombie after studying for the cloud certification all night.

mis.bad: Kill the process zombie in Linux.
mis.good: Kill the zombie process in Linux.
mis.why: Noun adjuncts precede the head noun in English: "zombie process".

def: The division of land into zones for different purposes, such as residential or commercial.
ex: Municipal zoning laws prevent high-rise commercial office developments from opening inside quiet residential neighborhoods.
nat: The property developer applied for a municipal zoning variance to build affordable apartment units.

mis.bad: The city changed the laws of zoning.
mis.good: The city changed the zoning laws.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "zoning laws", not "laws of zoning".
